reviewBoundary: Three complete junior reading practices: four four-question passages plus a four-email/five-question thread and separate five-question reading. Fictional cases; same-author evidence/all-alternative review, not independent calibration.

units.title: A radio programme and a quilt
units.alignmentNote: Two complete written four-question passages for junior2 explicitly adapt the written-reading part of its source. Junior3 retains a four-email thread with five questions plus a separate five-question reading, all three-choice. No source prose copied.

materials.title: The sound between songs
materials.text:
My grandfather keeps a small radio on his kitchen shelf. When I stayed with him last summer, I expected him to play music throughout breakfast. Instead, he often listened to people talking about events in the town.

One morning, a presenter described an old dance hall that was about to reopen. Grandpa turned the sound up. He had worked there on Saturday evenings when he was young, carrying chairs and selling tickets at the door. He had never been a musician, although I had imagined him playing in a band.

The presenter invited listeners to share memories. Grandpa did not phone immediately. He wrote down a few points and checked a date in an old diary. He remembered a particular winter party clearly, but the year was uncertain until he found the entry.

When he called later, the presenter asked about one small detail: what happened to wet coats? Grandpa explained the row of numbered hooks and the paper tickets people kept to claim their clothes. I had expected a story about famous performers. Instead, the conversation showed how the place worked for an ordinary visitor.

Afterwards, we walked past the hall. Its windows were covered while repairs continued, but I could imagine the queue and the coat hooks inside. Grandpa's contribution had lasted only two minutes on the radio. It had changed the building for me from an empty address into a place where people had spent their evenings.

questions.prompt: What does Grandpa often listen to at breakfast?
options: Recorded school examinations
Local discussion programmes
Lessons about building radios
Only live music from his own band
questions.explanation: He listens to talk about town events. His own band is imagined and the other programmes are not mentioned.

questions.prompt: Why does he look at an old diary?
options: To find a musician’s telephone number
To confirm the year of a remembered party
To learn how to switch the radio on
To order new chairs for the hall
questions.explanation: He checks the uncertain year. Numbers, ordering and radio operation are not the reason.

questions.prompt: What detail does the presenter ask about?
options: Who repaired the radio
How visitors’ wet coats were managed
Which famous singer owned the building
Why every ticket was free
questions.explanation: Coat storage and numbered tickets form the interview detail. Famous ownership/free admission/radio repair are invented.

questions.prompt: How does the narrator see the hall afterwards?
options: As a place connected with ordinary people’s experiences
As a working radio shop
As a building whose history is now completely known
As a place Grandpa never entered
questions.explanation: The hall gains lived meaning through a partial memory. Grandpa worked there; it is no radio shop and a two-minute account is not total history.

materials.title: The squares in the cupboard
materials.text:
When our community centre made a quilt for its new room, each family was invited to contribute one fabric square. The notice gave a fixed size so that the pieces could be joined, but left the colours and patterns to the contributors.

My mother found a piece from an old curtain. I thought we should buy something new. She showed me a photograph of our first flat, where the curtain had hung beside my baby chair. The fabric suddenly seemed less ordinary, though the square itself could not explain that history.

We wrote a short note to accompany it. Other families did the same. One square came from a shirt, another from unused cloth kept for years. Nobody had to contribute a personal object; a newly bought square was welcome too.

At the sewing session, volunteers checked the sizes before joining anything. Two pieces needed an extra border to fit. The volunteers asked their owners before altering them and kept the pattern visible. The finished quilt was planned as a shared object, not a competition for the most unusual square.

The notes were placed in a folder beside the quilt. Visitors could enjoy the whole design first, then discover some of the stories behind it. I liked that arrangement. Our small piece remained part of our family history, but it also belonged to a new pattern that no family had made alone.

questions.prompt: What does the notice fix?
options: The age of every fabric
The size of each square
Every family’s colour choice
The story each family must tell
questions.explanation: Size is fixed for assembly. Colours/patterns are open, old/new fabric allowed and stories not prescribed.

questions.prompt: Why does the curtain fabric matter to the family?
options: It belonged to their first flat
It was bought by every contributor
It is the only new cloth in the town
It can tell its own story without a note
questions.explanation: The photograph establishes the family connection. Newness/universal purchase/self-explanation are contradicted or unsupported.

questions.prompt: What happens to pieces needing adjustment?
options: They are thrown away immediately
Owners are asked before borders are added
Their owners must leave the project
Their patterns are completely covered
questions.explanation: Consent and visible pattern are stated. Disposal/erasure/exclusion do not occur.

questions.prompt: Why keep the notes beside the quilt?
options: To replace the quilt with a written report
To offer individual stories alongside the shared design
To prove that only old cloth is valuable
To rank the families by spending
questions.explanation: The folder adds provenance without replacing the design. Ranking and old-only value are explicitly absent.

units.title: A visiting dog and a paper model
units.alignmentNote: Two complete written four-question passages for junior2 explicitly adapt the written-reading part of its source. Junior3 retains a four-email thread with five questions plus a separate five-question reading, all three-choice. No source prose copied.

materials.title: A visit with Milo
materials.text:
My aunt brought her dog Milo when she stayed with us. He was friendly, but our busy home was new to him. My younger brother wanted to introduce every toy and every room on the first afternoon.

Aunt Rosa asked us to slow down. She set Milo's bed in a quiet corner and showed us how to leave him space. He could come towards us when ready. At first, my brother thought this meant the visit would be boring. He sat on the carpet with a book and waited.

After a while, Milo walked over and lay nearby. My brother began reading aloud, using a different voice for each character. The dog did not understand the story in the way a person would, but he remained settled beside the familiar voice. My brother forgot to demand a game.

Later, Aunt Rosa took Milo out for his usual walk. We went with her rather than trying to change every part of his day. She explained which places were suitable and kept control of his lead. We were visitors to his routine as much as he was a visitor to our house.

By the end of the weekend, my brother had filled a page with drawings of Milo sleeping, walking and looking through the window. None showed the dog wearing a toy hat or performing a trick. The visit had been interesting after all. Paying attention had given him more to remember than trying to arrange entertainment every minute.

questions.prompt: What does the younger brother first want?
options: To send Milo home at once
To leave the house for the weekend
To hide all his toys forever
To show Milo everything immediately
questions.explanation: He wants an immediate tour and toy introduction. Rejection/permanent hiding/departure are not his initial plan.

questions.prompt: Why is Milo’s bed put in a quiet corner?
options: To stop him ever seeing the family
To hide a broken carpet
To give him space in the unfamiliar home
To prepare a stage for tricks
questions.explanation: The quiet base gives a new visitor space. Permanent isolation/tricks/carpet concealment are not stated.

questions.prompt: How is the walk arranged?
options: Milo chooses to travel by himself
The walk is cancelled for games
The children take Milo alone to every new place
Aunt Rosa follows his routine and controls the lead
questions.explanation: The aunt leads the usual walk and supervises suitable places. The alternatives contradict that.

questions.prompt: What do the brother’s drawings suggest?
options: He has forgotten the visit entirely
He only values tricks and costumes
He has become interested in Milo’s ordinary behaviour
He never looked at the dog
questions.explanation: Sleeping/walking/window drawings show attentive interest. Tricks/costumes are specifically absent; observation and memory are present.

materials.title: The paper model that would not stand
materials.text:
For a class display, I made a paper model of our town library. It had windows, a tiny sign and a roof that looked almost exactly like the real building. When I put it on the table, it leaned to one side.

I tried adding more colour to the sign, as though a better-looking front would make the model stand. My partner gently moved it away from the wall I had been using to support it. The whole side folded inward.

We looked at the instructions again. I had cut off two small tabs because I thought they were waste paper. They should have connected the side to the base. The problem was not a lack of decoration but a missing connection.

Our teacher allowed us to make a new base from spare card. We drew and measured it before cutting. This time, I left the tabs in place and checked how they folded before using glue. We also tried standing the model without its roof so we could see what happened inside.

The repaired library did not look quite as neat underneath. A join was visible if someone lifted it. But it stood on its own and could be carried to the display. I put the first cut piece beside it, with a note about the missing tabs. The mistake became part of our explanation of how the model was built, rather than something hidden behind its colourful front.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with the first model?
options: It is made entirely from wood
It cannot stand securely without support
It is larger than the real library
It has no windows or sign
questions.explanation: It leans and folds when wall support is removed. Windows/sign exist, and it is a paper miniature.

questions.prompt: Why are the tabs important?
options: They name all the books inside
They make the building taller than a person
They connect the side to the base
They provide extra paint for the roof
questions.explanation: Their structural connecting role is explained. Decoration/book naming/huge height are not their purpose.

questions.prompt: What does the narrator do differently with the new base?
options: Cuts off every tab again
Checks the tabs and folds before gluing
Only paints the sign more brightly
Uses the wall as permanent support
questions.explanation: Measuring and checking folds precede glue. The earlier errors are not repeated.

questions.prompt: Why is the first piece displayed too?
options: To help explain the construction mistake
To claim the first model had been perfect
To hide the repaired model from visitors
To ask visitors to take it home
questions.explanation: It illustrates missing tabs with an explanatory note. Perfection/concealment/giveaway are not the intent.

units.title: A film screening and a changing title
units.alignmentNote: Two complete written four-question passages for junior2 explicitly adapt the written-reading part of its source. Junior3 retains a four-email thread with five questions plus a separate five-question reading, all three-choice. No source prose copied.

materials.title: Four messages about the short-film screening
materials.text:
From: Ms Patel
Sent: Monday, 08:30
To: Film club helpers
Subject: Friday screening
We will show the students' short films in Room 12 on Friday. Helpers should arrive at 15:30, and the audience enters at 16:00. The screening ends at 17:10. Please bring your club badge. We will provide the programme sheets and equipment. Each film will be introduced by its student director.

From: Lina
Sent: Tuesday, 18:00
To: Ms Patel and helpers
Subject: Re: Friday screening
My film lasts six minutes, but the title in the draft programme is wrong. It should be The Empty Platform, not The Last Platform. Please change the sheet before printing. I can introduce it myself, but I will need to leave at 17:00. I cannot help clear the room after the final film.

From: Ms Patel
Sent: Wednesday, 11:00
To: Film club helpers
Subject: Room and programme update
The projector in Room 12 is not working, so we have moved to the library hall. Arrival and screening times are unchanged. Lina's title has been corrected, and her film will be shown first so she can leave as planned. Omar has agreed to stay for clearing up. Do not print the old room number on any new signs.

From: Omar
Sent: Thursday, 16:45
To: Film club helpers
Subject: Final signs
I have put directions from Room 12 to the library hall in the programme folder. Please collect them when you arrive at 15:30. The sheets are already printed, so no more copies are needed. The library entrance closes at 16:15; late visitors must ring the bell at the side door. The screening still ends at 17:10, and I will help return the hall's chairs afterwards.

questions.prompt: Where will the films be screened?
options: In the library hall
In Room 12
At the side door
questions.explanation: Wednesday changes the venue to library hall. Room12 is obsolete, side door entry only.

questions.prompt: What is Lina’s film called?
options: The Empty Platform
The Last Platform
The Broken Projector
questions.explanation: Tuesday corrects the title to Empty, confirmed Wednesday.

questions.prompt: Why is Lina’s film shown first?
options: She needs to leave before the event ends
She has refused to introduce it
It is the only six-minute film allowed
questions.explanation: The order accommodates17:00 departure before17:10 end. Duration restriction/refusal are not stated.

questions.prompt: What should a visitor arriving at 16:20 do?
options: Wait in Room 12 for a separate screening
Enter through the closed library entrance
Ring the bell at the side door
questions.explanation: After16:15 the side-door bell is required. No second screening is offered.

questions.prompt: Who has agreed to help clear up?
options: Every late visitor
Lina after 17:10
Omar
questions.explanation: Omar volunteers and confirms chairs. Lina leaves earlier; visitors are not assigned cleanup.

materials.title: Three names for one story
materials.text:
I wrote a story for our class magazine and called it The Storm. The title seemed exciting, but my friend expected the whole story to be about dangerous weather. In fact, the storm ended after the first paragraph. Most of the story followed two neighbours trying to return a lost suitcase.

My teacher did not choose a new title for me. She asked what a reader would expect from the one I had written. I made a second list: The Suitcase, Two Neighbours and After the Rain. Each pointed towards a different part of the story.

The Suitcase named the central object, but it did not suggest much about the people. Two Neighbours emphasised the pair, although the owner of the case mattered too. After the Rain suggested the time and a change in mood, but did not mention the mystery. There was no title that explained every detail equally.

I read the opening and ending again. The final scene showed the neighbours sitting outside together after they had found the owner. They had lived next door for years without speaking much. The practical search had begun a friendship.

I chose After the Rain, not because the other titles were wrong in every way, but because it led towards the part I wanted to emphasise. In the magazine, one reader still said she had expected more weather. I listened to her explanation without changing the title immediately. A title offers a doorway into a story; it cannot control everything a reader imagines before entering.

questions.prompt: Why does The Storm create an unsuitable expectation for the friend?
options: The friend dislikes every exciting title
Weather is central only to the opening paragraph
The story contains no rain anywhere
questions.explanation: The storm soon ends and the search occupies most of the story. Rain exists and universal dislike is not claimed.

questions.prompt: What does the teacher ask the writer to consider?
options: Whether every story must name its weather
Which title has the most letters
What the title leads a reader to expect
questions.explanation: Reader expectation is the teacher’s question. Letter count and mandatory weather naming are not proposed.

questions.prompt: What does the suitcase search change?
options: The neighbours move to different countries
The owner loses the case a second time
The neighbours become friends
questions.explanation: The ending shows a new friendship after years of little conversation. Moving abroad/repeated loss are not stated.

questions.prompt: Why is After the Rain selected?
options: It describes every event in full
It emphasises the change the writer values
The teacher orders its use
questions.explanation: The writer selects emphasis and accepts incomplete coverage. The teacher does not choose, and no title covers everything.

questions.prompt: How does the writer respond to the later reader?
options: Refuses to hear any explanation
Claims a title controls every expectation
Listens without assuming an immediate change is necessary
questions.explanation: The ending describes listening while keeping the title for now. Refusal and complete control are explicitly rejected.
